also.hook: Andrew Barto earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics and a PhD in computer and communication sciences, both from the University of Michigan. In 1977 he joined the University of Massachusetts Amherst as a postdoctoral research associate and spent his career there, rising through associate professor and professor to department chair before becoming Professor Emeritus of Information and Computer Sciences. Beginning in the 1980s, working closely with Richard Sutton, he developed the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning, including temporal difference learning, policy gradient methods and agent designs that combine learning with planning. He and Sutton distilled that work into the textbook Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, first published in 1998 with a second edition in 2018, which became the standard reference for the field. In 2024 the Association for Computing Machinery awarded Barto and Sutton the ACM A.M. Turing Award for this body of work.
also.name: Andrew Barto
also.moniker: Professor Emeritus, University of Massachusetts Amherst

also.hook: Bernhard Schölkopf studied physics, mathematics and philosophy in Tübingen and London, then completed a doctorate in computer science at the Technical University of Berlin in 1997. He worked at the German National Research Center for Computer Science and held industrial research posts at AT&T Bell Laboratories, Microsoft Research and Biowulf Technologies, a period in which he helped develop the kernel methods that underlie the support vector machine framework used widely in machine learning. In 2001 he became a director and scientific member at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, and since 2011 he has directed the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Tübingen. His research has shifted toward causal machine learning, arguing that statistical learning methods need causal structure to generalize reliably outside their training distribution, work recognized with the 2019 Körber Prize. He also holds an honorary professorship at TU Berlin.
also.name: Bernhard Schölkopf
also.moniker: Director, Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems

also.hook: Bakalar leads AI ethics at OpenAI after nearly four years as Chief Ethicist at Meta, where she moved from Responsible AI research into leading ethics across GenAI Trust and Safety and Meta Superintelligence Labs. She holds a PhD in Political Science from the University of Pennsylvania and spent seven years on the faculty at Temple University before moving into industry.
also.name: Chloé Bakalar

also.hook: Christopher Ré runs Stanford's Hazy Research lab, which has spent more than a decade turning ideas about data quality and hardware efficiency into companies. His early work on DeepDive, a system for pulling structured facts out of unstructured dark data, won him a MacArthur Fellowship in 2015. He later co-founded Snorkel AI to make labeling training data programmatic instead of manual, and Together AI, alongside collaborators including Tri Dao, Ce Zhang and Percy Liang, to build infrastructure for training and running open foundation models. Along the way his lab's systems work on hardware-aware training has fed directly into how modern language models are trained and served at scale.
also.name: Christopher Ré
also.moniker: Professor of Computer Science, Stanford University, and Founder, Together AI and Snorkel AI

also.hook: Brynjolfsson has spent three decades building the empirical case for how digital technology, and now AI, actually changes productivity and jobs, work that shifted from academic papers to boardroom strategy as generative AI forced every company to ask the same question he had been measuring for years.
also.name: Erik Brynjolfsson
also.moniker: Economist of the Second Machine Age

also.hook: Li made modern AI's breakthrough possible by betting on data before it was fashionable: ImageNet's fourteen million labeled images gave the field the benchmark on which AlexNet proved deep learning worked. She has spent the years since insisting the technology stay pointed at people, building Stanford HAI and carrying the human-centered case into policy rooms from Sacramento to Washington.
also.name: Fei-Fei Li

also.hook: Hinton kept faith with neural networks through two AI winters, and won. The training method he championed in 1986 and the 2012 breakthrough his lab produced turned a marginal idea into the technology behind modern AI. Then, at the peak of vindication, he quit Google to warn the world about what he had helped build, giving AI risk its most credentialed voice.
also.name: Geoffrey Hinton

also.hook: Jerome Friedman trained as a physicist, earning a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley before working as a research physicist in high-energy physics. In 1972 he joined the Stanford Computation Research Group, and in 1982 he was appointed a professor of statistics at Stanford University. With Leo Breiman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees (CART), published in 1984, and in 1991 he introduced Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) in the Annals of Statistics. In 2001 he published Greedy Function Approximation, formalizing gradient boosting machines as a general method that later became central to widely used tools for structured data prediction. He also co-authored the textbook The Elements of Statistical Learning with Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, and is now Professor of Statistics, Emeritus, at Stanford.
also.name: Jerome Friedman
also.moniker: Professor of Statistics, Emeritus, Stanford University

also.hook: Jürgen Schmidhuber was born in Munich, Germany, and earned his doctorate in computer science from the Technical University of Munich in 1991. In 1990 he proposed an early adversarial training scheme in which two neural networks competed against each other, an idea later recognized as anticipating generative adversarial networks. In 1997 he and his student Sepp Hochreiter published Long Short-Term Memory, a recurrent neural network architecture that overcame the vanishing gradient problem and became one of the most widely used designs in speech recognition and language modeling before the rise of Transformers. He has long served as Scientific Director of the Swiss AI Lab IDSIA, and since 2021 has also directed the AI Initiative at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology. He co-founded NNAISENSE, a company applying his lab's neural network research to industrial and robotic systems.
also.name: Jürgen Schmidhuber
also.moniker: Scientific Director, Swiss AI Lab IDSIA

also.hook: Dixon became Chancellor of North Carolina Central University in 2024 after leading Elizabeth City State University for over eight years, including as interim and then permanent Chancellor, and after six years overseeing academic and student affairs system-wide for the 17-campus University of North Carolina system. Her research has focused on college access and summer bridge programs.
also.name: Karrie G. Dixon

also.hook: Michael I. Jordan earned a master's degree in mathematics from Arizona State University and a PhD in cognitive science from the University of California, San Diego in 1985. He joined the faculty of MIT in 1988, before moving to the University of California, Berkeley in 1998. At Berkeley he holds the Pehong Chen Distinguished Professorship jointly in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Department of Statistics. His research connects statistics, optimization and computer science, with major contributions to probabilistic graphical models, variational inference and Bayesian nonparametric methods that shaped how modern machine learning systems reason under uncertainty. He has also been an outspoken voice pushing back on hype around artificial general intelligence, arguing in his widely read 2018 essay that the field needs a genuine engineering discipline built around real world human centered systems rather than science fiction narratives about human imitative AI.
also.name: Michael I. Jordan
also.moniker: Pehong Chen Distinguished Professor, UC Berkeley

also.hook: Nick Bostrom is a Swedish philosopher who has shaped how both academics and the public think about the long term risks and possibilities of advanced technology. He trained across physics, computational neuroscience, and philosophy at the universities of Gothenburg, Stockholm, and King's College London, and completed a PhD in philosophy at the London School of Economics in 2000. In 2002 he published the paper Existential Risks, which introduced a systematic taxonomy of the ways humanity's long term potential could be destroyed or permanently curtailed. In 2005 he founded and directed the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University, building it from three researchers into a center that helped incubate the fields of AI safety and effective altruism before it closed in 2024. His 2014 book Superintelligence, Paths, Dangers, Strategies became a New York Times bestseller and is widely credited with moving concerns about advanced AI from niche discussion into mainstream academic and public debate. He continues this work as founder of the Macrostrategy Research Initiative, and published the book Deep Utopia in 2024.
also.name: Nick Bostrom
also.moniker: Philosopher of existential risk and superintelligence

also.hook: Katti built his career on the unglamorous but essential problem of moving data efficiently, first in academic networking research, then running Intel's networking hardware division, and now at OpenAI, where the physical compute infrastructure behind frontier AI models is his direct responsibility.
also.name: Sachin Katti
also.moniker: OpenAI's Head of Compute and Former Stanford Networking Professor

also.hook: Thrun proved autonomous driving was possible by winning DARPA's toughest robotics prize, then built the Google program that turned that proof into Waymo, the industry's leading self-driving company, while separately co-founding Udacity to bring university-grade technical education online.
also.name: Sebastian Thrun
also.moniker: Founder of Google's Self-Driving Car Project and Udacity

also.hook: Stuart Russell is Distinguished Professor of Computer Science at UC Berkeley, where he also holds the Smith-Zadeh Professorship in Engineering and a professorship in Cognitive Science. With Peter Norvig he co-authored Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, first published in 1995 and now in multiple editions, which became the standard textbook used to teach AI in universities worldwide. In 2016 he founded the Center for Human-Compatible AI (CHAI) at Berkeley, a research lab devoted to redesigning AI systems around explicit uncertainty about human preferences rather than fixed objectives, on the argument that optimizing a fixed goal too well is what makes highly capable AI systems dangerous. He set out that argument for a general audience in his 2019 book Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control, and in 2021 he delivered the BBC's Reith Lectures on living with artificial intelligence. He holds an OBE and is a Fellow of the Royal Society, and also serves as Professor of Computational Precision Health at UCSF and an Honorary Fellow of Wadham College, Oxford.
also.name: Stuart Russell
also.moniker: Distinguished Professor of Computer Science, UC Berkeley

also.hook: Takeo Kanade earned his PhD in electrical engineering from Kyoto University in 1974 and taught there before joining Carnegie Mellon University in 1980. He directed Carnegie Mellon's Robotics Institute from 1992 to 2001 and now holds the title of U.A. and Helen Whitaker University Professor of Robotics and Computer Science there. Across a research career spanning computer vision and robotics, he pioneered early facial recognition methods, multi-baseline stereo vision, the factorization method for recovering 3D shape and motion from images, and virtualized reality techniques for capturing 3D scenes from multiple cameras. He also led Carnegie Mellon's Navlab autonomous vehicle program, including a 1995 cross-country demonstration drive in which the vehicle steered itself for most of the route from Pittsburgh to San Diego. In 2016 he received the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology for his contributions to the field.
also.name: Takeo Kanade
also.moniker: Computer vision and robotics pioneer, Carnegie Mellon University

also.hook: Tom Mitchell helped establish machine learning as an academic discipline in its own right. He earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from MIT in 1973 and a PhD from Stanford University in 1979, studying under Bruce Buchanan. After teaching at Rutgers University, he joined Carnegie Mellon University in 1986, where he became the E. Fredkin Professor and later the founding chair of the world's first Machine Learning Department in 2006. In 1997 he published the textbook Machine Learning, one of the first comprehensive textbooks in the field and still used in university courses. His later research pushed machine learning into new territory, including the Never-Ending Language Learner project, which continuously extracts facts from web text, and work using brain imaging to study how the brain represents word meaning. He has also studied the effects of AI on the labor market, co-chairing a National Academies report on AI and the future of work.
also.name: Tom Mitchell
also.moniker: University Professor, Carnegie Mellon University Machine Learning Department

profiles.hook: Ng did more than any single figure to turn machine learning from a graduate-school subject into a skill anyone could learn online, while simultaneously building the industrial-scale infrastructure, Google Brain among it, that made deep learning practical at big-tech scale.
profiles.name: Andrew Ng
profiles.moniker: AI Educator and Deep Learning Pioneer

profiles.hook: Anima Anandkumar is a computer scientist known for pioneering the use of tensor decomposition methods to give provable guarantees for learning latent variable models, an alternative to techniques that lacked theoretical grounding. She earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras in 2004 and a PhD in electrical and computer engineering from Cornell University in 2009, followed by a postdoctoral position at MIT. She then built an academic career at the University of California, Irvine, rising from assistant to associate professor, before moving into industry as a principal scientist at Amazon AI and later as director and then senior director of AI research at NVIDIA. Since 2017 she has held the Bren Professorship in Computing and Mathematical Sciences at Caltech, where her group extends foundational machine learning theory into applied problems such as physics informed neural networks, weather forecasting and drug discovery. Her career bridges rigorous theoretical work on learning algorithms with large scale applied AI research built inside major technology companies.
profiles.name: Anima Anandkumar
profiles.moniker: Bren Professor of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, Caltech

profiles.hook: Percy Liang is a computer scientist whose work has shaped how the field measures and understands large language models. He earned a Bachelor of Science from MIT in 2004 and a PhD in computer science from the University of California, Berkeley in 2011, advised by Michael Jordan and Dan Klein. He joined the faculty of Stanford University, where he is a professor of computer science with a courtesy appointment in statistics, and became director of the Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models. In 2022 he led a large multi institution team in creating Holistic Evaluation of Language Models, a benchmarking framework designed to standardize how language models are assessed across accuracy, robustness, fairness and other dimensions at once. He has also built infrastructure for reproducible AI research, including CodaLab Worksheets, and teaches a widely followed Stanford course on building language models from scratch.
profiles.name: Percy Liang
profiles.moniker: Director, Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models

primary.name: Liang et al., Holistic Evaluation of Language Models, arXiv:2211.09110

profiles.hook: Terence Tao is a mathematician whose work spans harmonic analysis, partial differential equations, number theory and combinatorics, and who has more recently turned his attention to using computers and formal proof systems to assist mathematical research. He completed his PhD at Princeton University in 1996 under Elias Stein and joined UCLA the same year, where he has been a full professor since 2000 and has held the James and Carol Collins Chair in Mathematics since 2007. In 2006 he received the Fields Medal, mathematics' highest honor, for contributions across several areas of analysis and combinatorics. In November 2023, after co-authoring a proof of the Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture over finite fields with Tim Gowers, Ben Green and Freddie Manners, Tao led a rapid collaborative effort with Yael Dillies and Bhavik Mehta to formalize the entire proof in the Lean 4 proof assistant using a tool called Blueprint, completing the verification within weeks. He has continued to build public infrastructure for formalized mathematics, including a Lean companion to his own real analysis textbook and, in 2026, a registry called Palomar for tracking Lean verified proofs amid a rise in AI generated mathematical claims.
profiles.name: Terence Tao

profiles.hook: Yejin Choi is a computer scientist known for advancing commonsense reasoning and evaluation methods in natural language processing. She earned a bachelor's degree in computer engineering from Seoul National University and a PhD in computer science from Cornell University, then built her academic career at the University of Washington, where she held the Brett Helsel Career Development Professorship from 2020 to 2023 and the Wissner-Slivka Chair from 2023 to 2024. Her research has focused on giving machines the kind of everyday, common sense knowledge that humans take for granted, and on building benchmarks that reveal when large language models fail at reasoning tasks that seem simple to people. In 2022 she was named a MacArthur Fellow for this work and became an ACL Fellow the same year. She has since moved to Stanford University, where she holds the Dieter Schwarz Foundation Professorship in Computer Science and is a Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, continuing work on democratizing generative AI through smaller models and on pluralistic alignment of AI systems with diverse human values.
profiles.name: Yejin Choi
profiles.moniker: Dieter Schwarz Foundation Professor, Stanford University
